pages.metaDesc: A plain-English hub for high-visibility workwear — what EN ISO 20471 measures, the three classes, how to choose by road speed and environment, and the detailed guides.
pages.lede: "Hi-vis" isn't one thing — it's three classes, one standard, and a decision that hangs on how fast the traffic moves and how bad the light gets. This hub gives you the whole picture, then points to the detailed guides.

blocks.h2: Two materials, three classes, one decision
blocks.html:
High-visibility clothing works two ways at once. Fluorescent background fabric lifts the wearer out of the background in daylight; retroreflective tape bounces headlights back at drivers after dark. A compliant garment needs enough of both, and the standard that sets "enough" is EN ISO 20471.

That standard sorts garments into three classes by the minimum area of each material. More area = visibility at greater distance and worse light — so the class you need is driven by risk, chiefly the speed of nearby traffic and the light level.

blocks.lead: Class is set by the minimum area of fluorescent background and retroreflective material. Higher class = seen from further away.

items.p: Low-risk, off-road — car parks, warehouses away from traffic.
The everyday workhorse — typically a waistcoat or vest.
Maximum visibility — needs sleeves or trouser bands. High-speed roads, night work.

faq.q: What are the three hi-vis classes?
faq.a: EN ISO 20471 defines three classes by the minimum area of fluorescent background and retroreflective material. Class 1 is lowest, Class 2 sits in the middle (typically a vest), and Class 3 is highest and normally needs sleeves or trouser bands. Higher class means visibility over greater distance and in worse conditions.

faq.q: Which hi-vis class do I legally need?
faq.a: There's no single legal class — it's risk-led. High-speed roads, night work and highway maintenance point to Class 3; busy yards to Class 2; low-risk off-road to Class 1. Some sectors set their own rule — rail mandates orange Class 3.

faq.q: Does hi-vis stop being compliant over time?
faq.a: Yes. Fluorescence fades and tape degrades with washing, UV and wear, so a faded garment can drop below the standard even though it still looks yellow. Garments carry a maximum number of wash cycles — replace worn kit.

pages.metaDesc: What EN ISO 20471 measures — the fluorescent background and retroreflective areas behind Class 1, 2 and 3, the permitted colours, certification, and why the wash-cycle limit matters.
pages.lede: The standard behind every compliant hi-vis garment comes down to a simple idea: enough bright fabric to be seen by day, enough reflective tape to be seen at night. Here's exactly what it measures, and how the three classes fall out of it.

blocks.html:
EN ISO 20471 is the standard for high-visibility clothing for professional use. It sets performance for two materials that do different jobs:

  • Fluorescent background fabric — reacts with daylight UV to appear brighter than any natural colour, giving daytime conspicuity.
  • Retroreflective material — bounces headlights straight back to the driver, giving night-time visibility.

A garment must carry a minimum area of each, and both must meet minimum colour, luminance and retroreflection performance.

blocks.h2: Where the three classes come from
blocks.lead: The class is how much of each material the garment carries — minimum areas for the highest-performing garment in each class.
head: Class
Background (fluoro)
Retroreflective
Typical garment

blocks.html: Why a vest usually can't be Class 3: a sleeveless waistcoat can't hold 0.80 m² of background. Class 3 means sleeves, or a jacket + hi-vis trousers together — see Class 2 vs Class 3.

blocks.h2: Yellow, orange or red — and a UKCA/CE mark
blocks.html: Three fluorescent backgrounds are permitted — yellow, orange-red and red — each within defined colour and luminance limits. Rail and much highways work call for orange; general industry leans yellow. Because hi-vis is PPE, compliant garments carry a UKCA (or CE) mark with the standard reference.

Both materials degrade — fluorescent dye fades under UV and washing; tape cracks and dulls. So garments are marked with a maximum number of wash cycles. A garment past its rating, visibly faded, or with cracked tape should be treated as non-compliant and replaced, regardless of how yellow it looks.

faq.a: The minimum area of fluorescent background fabric (daytime conspicuity) and the minimum area of retroreflective material (night visibility). A garment's class depends on carrying enough of both, plus minimum photometric and colour performance.
Rarely. Class 3 needs about 0.80 m² of background, which a sleeveless waistcoat can't provide. Class 3 is achieved with sleeves, or by combining a compliant jacket with hi-vis trousers.
Fluorescent yellow, orange-red and red, each with defined colour and luminance limits. The choice is often driven by sector — rail and some highways work specify orange.

pages.metaDesc: Class 2 or Class 3 hi-vis? The real difference is coverage and when it's required — road speed, light level and machinery. A plain decision guide with a by-role table.
pages.lede: It's the most common hi-vis question, and the honest answer is a risk assessment — but the pattern is clear. The faster the traffic and the worse the light, the more it tips from a Class 2 vest to full Class 3.

blocks.lead: Both are EN ISO 20471. The gap is how much bright fabric and tape the garment carries — and therefore how far away, and in how little light, you're seen.

items.p: Typically a vest. Good day / moderate-light visibility. Busy yards, deliveries, car parks. Lighter and cheaper — but short where speed and dark combine.
Needs sleeves, or jacket + hi-vis trousers. Seen from further and in poor light. Required for high-speed roads, night work, highways. The safe default near live traffic.

blocks.html: Why sleeves matter: the jump to 0.80 m² is usually impossible in a vest, so Class 3 means a sleeved garment or a jacket + trousers together. Mechanics in EN ISO 20471 explained.

blocks.html: Rule of thumb: on or beside a live, higher-speed carriageway, or in the dark near moving vehicles — Class 3. Otherwise Class 2 is the sensible, wearable default, confirmed by your assessment.

faq.q: What's the difference between Class 2 and Class 3?
faq.a: Coverage. Class 2 carries about 0.50 m² of background and is typically a vest. Class 3 carries about 0.80 m² and normally needs sleeves or hi-vis trousers, making the wearer visible from further and in worse light. Class 3 is the higher level.

Where risk is highest — high-speed roads, highway maintenance, night or low-light work, and jobs around fast-moving vehicles. Railway trackside mandates orange Class 3. When speed and poor light combine, Class 3 is the safe default.

faq.q: Is Class 2 ever enough near roads?
faq.a: For low to moderate-speed, well-lit environments — busy yards, car parks, delivery work — Class 2 is often appropriate. The moment speed rises, light drops, or the work moves onto the live carriageway, the assessment usually points to Class 3.
